subject: science
intro: I'm Mr. Nakamura. Let's plan a hands-on simulation lesson on natural selection.

beats.narration: The simulation's central tool, the beaks, is right in the title.
This standard asks students to explain how genetic variation leads to some individuals surviving and reproducing more.
"Over generations" is essential; this is about populations, not individuals.
beats.text: Students will be able to explain how variation in traits leads to differences in survival and reproduction, causing populations to change over generations.

beats.narration: Darwin's finches connect to the historical story.
beats.text: Show photos of Galápagos finches with different beaks. "Why might these birds have such different beaks?"

beats.narration: The "trying to adapt" misconception is persistent, so I address it head-on.
beats.text: Explain the four parts of natural selection: variation, inheritance, overproduction, and differential survival. Correct the misconception that individuals "try" to adapt.

beats.narration: Graphing the population shift over rounds makes change over generations visible.
beats.text: Beak simulation: students get a "beak" (tweezers, spoon, clothespin, or chopsticks) and gather "food" (beans, rice, marbles) for 3 rounds. Low gatherers "die" and switch to a more successful beak. Graph the population over rounds.

beats.narration: Their own data becomes the evidence.
beats.text: Using your graph, explain why the population of spoon beaks changed. Use the words "variation" and "survive."

outro: Photos, framework, simulation, graph. Now you plan.
